title: Reading input with cin
learningGoals: read two values in one line
use the right arrows for input and output

youtube.title: C++ Input with cin: Ask the User a Question | C++ Programming EP 06
youtube.description: In this episode you will read a number with cin, read two values in one line and use the right arrows for input and output, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Reading input with cin · 0:45 Ask for an age · 1:25 Data flows through arrows · 1:55 Second program · 2:55 Recap · 3:26 Bug of the Day · 4:14 Challenge · 4:34 Next episode

thumbnail.visual: big text "ASK WITH CIN" in tomato on pastel blue; Xecxec next to a speech bubble that asks a question; thin black border and drop shadow.
thumbnail.pose: Xecxec next to a speech bubble that asks a question

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today your program learns to listen. It asks a question, waits, and then uses your answer.

scenes.onScreen: "Reading input with cin": numbered lines (1. cout sends data out; 2. cin brings data in; 3. The arrows show the direction) and an analogy card: a ticket counter: the program asks, and you answer through the window
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: Cout sends data out to the screen. Cin brings data in from the keyboard. The arrows show the direction of the data. For cout, the arrows point toward cout. For cin, they point toward the variable. Think of a ticket counter. The clerk asks where you go, and you answer.

analogy.title: Reading input with cin
analogy.body: A ticket counter: the program asks, and you answer through the window

scenes.onScreen: age.cpp: the program asks for an age and adds one
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 5] First we make an int called age. [HL 6] Then we print a question. There is no endl, so the cursor stays on the same line. [HL 7] Now cin reads a number from the keyboard and stores it in age. The arrows point at the variable. [HL 8] Last, we print age plus one. The program waits at line seven until you press Enter.

code.output: Enter your age: Next year you will be 18

scenes.onScreen: a flow of data from the keyboard into the variable
scenes.animation: Steps drop in left to right with a pop; connecting arrows draw on; the active step glows butter
scenes.narration: Follow the data. You type a number on the keyboard. The cin tool reads it. The variable age stores it. Then cout prints a new number built from age.

diagram.caption: a flow of data from the keyboard into the variable

scenes.onScreen: sum.cpp: one cin line reads two numbers
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 5] We make two ints in one line. [HL 7] One cin line reads both numbers. Type them with a space between. [TRACK a=4] The first number goes into a. [TRACK b=9] The second number goes into b. [HL 8] Then we print the sum, which is thirteen.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as sum dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. Type four, a space, and nine. Then press Enter. The program prints the sum.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. Cout sends data out, and cin brings data in. Two. The arrows point in the direction of the data. Three. Cin stores the typed value in a variable. Four. One cin line can read many values. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: Cout sends data out, and cin brings data in.
The arrows point in the direction of the data.
Cin stores the typed value in a variable.
One cin line can read many values.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: The arrows point the wrong way
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the g++ error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. Here cin has arrows that point at cin. The compiler says no match for operator, with a long list. Do not panic. The first line is the clue. Cin needs arrows that point at the variable. Change them, and the program builds.

scenes.onScreen: Why did the program wait for the user? It had a lot of input about commitment.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: Why did the program wait for the user? It had a lot of input about commitment.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: ask for two numbers and print their product
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Ask the user for the length and width of a room. Print the area. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: Next time: operators and expressions. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
Compiler output (exactly as g++ prints it):

age.cpp: In function 'int main()':
age.cpp:7:9: error: no match for 'operator<<' (operand types are 'std::istream' {aka 'std::basic_istream<char>'} and 'int')
    7 |     cin << age;
      |     ~~~ ^~ ~~~
      |     |      |
      |     |      int
bug.why: The arrows for cin point right, toward the variable. The arrows for cout point left, toward the stream.

pun: "Why did the program wait for the user? It had a lot of input about commitment."
challenge: Ask the user for the length and width of a room. Print the area.
challengeAnswer: Read two ints with one cin line. Print length times width, for example four times nine gives thirty-six.
